subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: A random variable X has its range {0, 1, 2} and the probabilities are P(X = 0) = 3c³, P(X = 1) = 4c − 10c², P(X = 2) = 5c − 1, where c is a constant. Find (i) c (ii) P(0 < X < 3) (iii) P(1 < X ≤ 2) (iv) P(X < 1).

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.42 — LAQ chapter 5 Random Variables, answer 45. (In this part of the scan book page = PDF page − 1: book p.42 was read at PDF p.43, not p.44 as the −2 rule predicts.) Printed appearances: AP 15, 20 · TS 15, 17. THE SPLIT IS THE BOOK'S: this is the only answer in the chapter that prints [N Marks] tags — [1 Mark] against the cubic 3c³ − 10c² + 9c − 2 = 0, [1 Mark] against the factorisation (c − 1)(c − 2)(3c − 1), [1 Mark] against 'c = 1/3 is the only possible value', [2 Marks] against (ii), [1 Mark] against (iii), [1 Mark] against (iv) — 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 7. The book rejects c = 1 and c = 2 with the bare remark '∵ 0 ≤ p ≤ 1'; the card shows WHICH probability breaks for each rejected root (P(X = 2) = 4 and 9), which is what the mark is for. The LAQ chapter header (book p.40) carries ★★★ and reads '7 Marks'; that ★★★ is the CHAPTER's rank, not this question's. Paper position: Maths-2A Section C runs Q18–Q24 at 7 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Q24 is the Random Variables slot, and this question IS Q24 of the book's Model Paper 2 (book p.114). Book's printed values recompute: c = 1/3, 8/9, 2/3, 1/9. No two-book check and no board back-test exist for this paper — recorded, not hidden. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would find c and the three probabilities — what equation c satisfies, how you solve it, why two roots are rejected, and which values of X each probability covers.
insider_note: One full mark is the rejection line: test c = 1 and c = 2 against P(X = 2) = 5c − 1, show the values 4 and 9 cannot be probabilities, and only then keep c = 1/3 — a bare c = 1/3 with no reason is a half answer.

steps.label: Write ΣP = 1 as a cubic
steps.margin_note: First mark (the book's own [1 Mark]). The three probabilities add to 1. Move the 1 across and order the powers: 3c³ − 10c² + 9c − 2 = 0. The constant term is −2, not −1 — the −1 from P(X = 2) and the −1 moved from the right side combine.

recall.must_convey: That the three probabilities add to 1, giving the cubic 3c³ − 10c² + 9c − 2 = 0.

sum of P equals one and collect terms into a cubic in c
three c cube minus ten c square plus nine c minus two is zero
moodu probabilities kalipithe one, cubic equation vastundi three c cube minus ten c square plus nine c minus two

steps.why: ΣP = 1 is the only condition the question gives, and here it is a cubic in c — three candidate values, of which the later steps must pick one. Getting the constant −2 right is what makes c = 1 a root.
common_mistakes: Ending with −1 instead of −2 as the constant term.
Writing 3c³ − 10c² + 9c − 1 = 0 and finding no rational root.

steps.label: Factorise the cubic
steps.margin_note: Second mark (book's [1 Mark]). The coefficients 3 − 10 + 9 − 2 add to 0, so c = 1 is a root. Synthetic division by 1 gives the quotient 3c² − 7c + 2, which factors as (c − 2)(3c − 1). Three roots: 1, 2, 1/3.

recall.must_convey: That c = 1 is a root because the coefficients add to zero, and the cubic factors as (c − 1)(c − 2)(3c − 1), giving c = 1, 2, 1/3.
accept: coefficients add to zero so c equals one is a root, divide out and factor to get c equals one two or one by three

heard_as: three c squared minus seven c plus two

steps.why: A cubic with a rational root is solved by finding that root and dividing it out. The coefficient-sum test is the fastest way to see c = 1, and it is the step this mark is given for.
common_mistakes: Trying c = 1/3 first by guesswork and never showing why.
Making an arithmetic slip in the synthetic division (3, −7, 2 is the quotient).

steps.label: Reject c = 1 and c = 2
steps.margin_note: Third mark (book's [1 Mark]). A probability lies between 0 and 1. Test each root against P(X = 2) = 5c − 1: c = 1 gives 4, c = 2 gives 9 — both impossible. c = 1/3 gives 1/9, 2/9, 2/3, all valid and adding to 1. Write the rejections; the mark is for the reason, not for the value.
lines: Every probability must lie between 0 and 1.

recall.must_convey: That c = 1 and c = 2 make P(X = 2) = 4 and 9, greater than 1, so they are rejected, and c = 1/3 gives valid probabilities.

steps.why: The cubic is only a necessary condition; each root must also give probabilities inside [0, 1]. That check is a separate marked step because it is the only place the meaning of c is used.
common_mistakes: Writing 'c = 1/3' with no reason for dropping 1 and 2.
Rejecting c = 1 because 'it is too big' without testing a probability.
Testing only P(X = 0) = 3c³, which is 3 and 24 — also fine as a reason, but say it.

steps.label: Find P(0 < X < 3)
steps.margin_note: Two marks (book's [2 Marks]). 0 < X < 3 with range {0, 1, 2} means X = 1 or 2. Add the two expressions first — (4c − 10c²) + (5c − 1) = 9c − 10c² − 1 — then put c = 1/3: 3 − 10/9 − 1 = 8/9.

steps.why: The event is a set of values of X, and X has only three values, so 0 < X < 3 keeps two of them. Adding the expressions before substituting is fewer fractions than substituting twice.
common_mistakes: Including X = 0 or X = 3 (there is no X = 3).

steps.label: Find P(1 < X ≤ 2)
steps.margin_note: One mark (book's [1 Mark]). 1 < X ≤ 2 keeps only X = 2 — the left end is excluded, the right end included. P(X = 2) = 5c − 1 = 5/3 − 1 = 2/3.

recall.must_convey: That P(1 < X ≤ 2) is P(X = 2) alone, which is 5c − 1 = 2/3.
accept: P of one less than X less than or equal to two is just P of X equals two which is five c minus one equals two by three

steps.why: Reading a strict and a non-strict inequality on the same line is the skill being tested. With integer values, 1 < X ≤ 2 is exactly X = 2.
common_mistakes: Including X = 1 because 1 appears in the inequality.

steps.label: Find P(X < 1)
steps.margin_note: Last mark (book's [1 Mark]). X < 1 keeps only X = 0. P(X = 0) = 3c³ = 3(1/27) = 1/9. As a check, the three probabilities 1/9, 2/9, 2/3 add to 1.

steps.why: X < 1 on the range {0, 1, 2} is the single value 0. The cube of 1/3 is 1/27, and 3/27 = 1/9 — the same value found in the rejection step, which is the built-in check.
